author: Eusebius of Caesarea
occasion: Eusebius writes to Flacillus to present his completed refutation of Marcellus, explaining its structure and asking Flacillus to judge and supplement if needed. The letter accompanies the work; it does not explain why the response was brief.
argument: Eusebius states that his brief response to Marcellus' long-winded treatise was sufficient because Marcellus' errors were self-evident and already condemned. In his first two books he made the refutation evident from Marcellus' own words alone, without any counter-argument. Now, in addition to that exposure, he has brought forward the overthrow of the same points through the three books at hand. He contrasts Marcellus' claim to know one God with his own honor of the holy and blessed Trinity, presented concisely. He asks Flacillus to judge the work and fill any gaps as a brother would.

outline.move: Eusebius explains the structure of his refutation of Marcellus, contrasts his Trinitarian theology with Marcellus' view, and asks Flacillus to judge and supplement the work.

cast.name: Eusebius
cast.who: The author, bishop of Caesarea, writing in his own voice.

cast.name: Flacillus
cast.who: The addressee of the letter, addressed as 'brother' (ἀδελφὸς ἀδελφοῦ). The name 'Flacillus' does not appear in the source text.

cast.name: Marcellus
cast.who: The opponent whose verbose writing Eusebius is refuting; accused of failing to give the Son of God a distinct subsistence.

voices.speaker: Marcellus (reported opponent)
voices.how_marked: His words are referred to indirectly as 'the man's words' (τοῦ ἀνδρὸς ῥημάτων), and his claim is reported with 'he says' (φησίν). No actual quotation of Marcellus' words appears in this letter; only indirect report and paraphrase.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The letter does not explain why the response was brief.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ δὴ πολλῶν ἔδει λόγων πρὸς ἀνατροπὴν τῶν αὐτόθεν καὶ τοῖς τυχοῦσιν κατεγνωσμένων
_unresolved_facts.fix: The letter explicitly explains why the response was brief: because Marcellus' errors were self-evident and already condemned by all, so many words were not needed.

_unresolved_facts.claim: In his first two books he made the refutation evident from Marcellus' own words alone, without any counter-argument.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐν δυσὶ τοῖς πρώτοις μόνῃ τῇ παραθέσει τῶν τοῦ ἀνδρὸς ῥημάτων χρησάμενος δίχα πάσης ἀντιρρήσεως
_unresolved_facts.fix: In the first two books Eusebius used only the juxtaposition/setting-forth of Marcellus' own words, without any counter-argument (ἀντίρρησις). 'Refutation' (ἔλεγχον) was the result, but the method was παράθεσις (juxtaposition/setting forth), not direct refutation.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Now, in addition to that exposure, he has brought forward the overthrow of the same points through the three books at hand.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: νυνὶ δὲ πρὸς ἐκείνῃ τῇ φώρᾳ καὶ τὴν ἀνατροπὴν τῶν αὐτῶν διὰ τριῶν τῶν μετὰ χεῖρας προσήγαγον
_unresolved_facts.fix: Now, in addition to that exposure (φώρα), he has brought forward the overthrow (ἀνατροπή) of the same points through the three books at hand. The brief says 'three books at hand' but should clarify Eusebius is referring to three additional books (making five total: two first books + three now at hand).

_unresolved_facts.claim: He contrasts Marcellus' claim to know one God with his own honor of the holy and blessed Trinity, presented concisely.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὁ μὲν γὰρ ἕν τι διωλύγιον καὶ πολυπλανὲς σύγγραμμα συντάξας τοῦτό φησιν πεποιηκέναι διὰ τὸ ἕνα γνωρίζειν θεόν, μή πη λάθῃ τῷ υἱῷ τοῦ θεοῦ χώραν διδοὺς ὑποστάσεως διελὼν τὴν γραφήν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Marcellus' claim is more specific: he says he wrote his long and wandering work 'in order to know one God, lest he unwittingly give the Son of God room for a distinct subsistence (ὑπόστασις), dividing the scripture.' Eusebius' concern is that Marcellus denies the Son a distinct subsistence. The contrast is between Marcellus' monarchian concern (fear of dividing God) and Eusebius' Trinitarian theology.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The name 'Flacillus' does not appear in the source text.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Remove this claim or clarify: while the name 'Flacillus' does not appear in the preserved text, the addressee is addressed throughout in the second person singular (κρίνειας, ἀναπληρώσειας).

_unresolved_facts.claim: No actual quotation of Marcellus' words appears in this letter; only indirect report and paraphrase.
_unresolved_facts.fix: This is accurate but should note that τοῦ ἀνδρὸς ῥημάτων ('the man's words') in the first two books implies direct quotation of Marcellus' words was used there, though not in this letter.
